title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

title: Math 107 Final exam practice
text:
A. Unit I refresh (Midterm 1 style)
Vectors, geometry, linear functions, neighbors / clustering, span and basis. Show work on computations.

Definitions and meaning
A1. What is a linear combination of vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\)?
A2. Define the inner product of two \(n\)-vectors. When are two vectors orthogonal?
A3. When is \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) linear? How does affine differ?
A4. Write formulas for \(\lVert x\rVert\) and the distance between \(x\) and \(y\). Write cosine similarity of nonzero \(a\) and \(b\).
A5. What is a basis of a subspace \(V\)? What is \(\dim V\)?
A6. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) is small, then \(\angle(a,b)\) must be near \(0\).”
A7. For each expression, say whether the result is a scalar, an \(n\)-vector, a set of vectors, or undefined (brief reason if undefined). Assume sizes make sense unless noted.

\(a^{\mathsf{T}}b\) for \(n\)-vectors \(a,b\)
\(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\)
\(a^{\mathsf{T}}b+c\) when \(c\) is an \(n\)-vector
unit vector \(a/\lVert a\rVert\) when \(a\neq 0\)



Computational
A8. Let \(u=(3,-1,2)\) and \(v=(0,4,-1)\). Compute \(u+v\), \(2u-v\), and \(u^{\mathsf{T}}v\).
A9. Write \(w=(5,1)\) as a linear combination of \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).
A10. Let \(x=(2,1,-1)\). Compute \(\lVert x\rVert\) exactly. Distance from \(p=(1,1)\) to \(q=(4,-3)\)?
A11. Cosine of the angle between \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\). Unit vector in the direction of \((3,4)\)?
A12. Is \(f(x)=3x_1-x_2+2\) linear or affine? Brief reason.
A13. Query \(x=(1,2)\); candidates \(z_1=(0,2)\), \(z_2=(3,2)\), \(z_3=(1,3)\). Which is nearest in Euclidean distance? Give the three distances.
A14. Points \(x_1=(0,0)\), \(x_2=(0,2)\), \(x_3=(6,0)\), \(x_4=(6,2)\); representatives \(z_1=(1,1)\), \(z_2=(5,1)\). Assign each point to the nearest \(z_j\), then update each \(z_j\) to the mean of its points.
A15. Are \((1,2)\) and \((-2,-4)\) linearly independent? Give a dependence relation or argue independence.
A16. Let \(V=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,0)\}\). Is \((2,3,2)\) in \(V\)? Is \((1,1,0)\) in \(V\)? What is \(\dim V\)?

title: Math 107 Final exam practice
text:
B. Unit II refresh (Midterm 2 style)
Matrices, \(Ax\), systems, dynamics, products, inverses, rank, determinants.

Definitions and meaning
B1. Give the column view formula for \(Ax\) when \(A\) has columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\).
B2. Translate “\(Ax=b\) has a solution” into a statement about \(C(A)\).
B3. When does \(Ax=b\) have (i) no solution, (ii) a unique solution, (iii) infinitely many solutions? Answer in RREF language.
B4. Write the model for a linear dynamical system used in class. How does \(A^k x_0\) relate?
B5. Define \(C(A)\), \(N(A)\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\). How do rank and \(\dim N(A)\) relate for an \(m\times n\) matrix?
B6. For \(\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{bmatrix}\), write \(\det A\). What does \(|\det A|\) mean for the unit square?
B7. True or false: “If \(\det A=0\), then \(A\) is invertible.” One-line reason.


Computational
B8. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&2\\ 0&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) using the column-combination view. Input and output dimensions of \(x\mapsto Ax\)?
B9. Let \[
R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(R e_1\) and \(R e_2\). Geometric effect?
B10. Write \[
\begin{aligned}
x+2y&=5,\\
3x-y&=1
\end{aligned}
\] as \(Ax=b\) and solve. How many solutions?
B11. The augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\) row-reduces to \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Identify pivot / free variables and write the general solution.
B12. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix},\quad
x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and \(x_2=Ax_1\). Express \(x_3\) using a matrix power.
B13. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(AB\) and \(BA\). Are they equal? Compute \(A^2\).
B14. Find the inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\) if it exists. Is \(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}\) invertible? Two reasons.
B15. The RREF of a \(3\times 4\) matrix \(A\) is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\), a basis for \(N(A)\), and check \(\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim N(A)=n\).
B16. Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\ 0&-3&4\\ 0&0&5\end{bmatrix}\).
B17. Cost: for large \(n\)-vectors \(a,b,c\), compare forming \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) versus \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\).

title: Math 107 Final exam practice
section: C. Since Midterm 2 (eigenvectors, complex, least squares, SVD)
text:
C. Since Midterm 2 (eigenvectors, complex, least squares, SVD)

Definitions and meaning
C1. What does it mean for nonzero \(v\) to be an eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\)?
C2. Write the characteristic equation for a square matrix \(A\).
C3. Interpret \(a+bi\) as a point in the complex plane. Compute \((1+2i)+(3-i)\) and \((1+2i)(3-i)\).
C4. Formulate the least-squares problem for \(Ax\approx b\). What is the residual?
C5. In one sentence: what does a rank-\(k\) SVD approximation keep, and what does it discard?
C6. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, then least squares has nothing to say.”
C7. True or false, with a one-line reason: “Every real \(2\times 2\) rotation matrix has a real eigenvector.”


Eigenpairs and complex arithmetic
C8. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix},\quad
v=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Verify that \(v\) is an eigenvector and find \(\lambda\).
C9. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\ 2&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] Form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) and find the eigenvalues. For the larger eigenvalue, find one eigenvector.
C10. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Compute \(A\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(A\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\). Does \(A\) look like a rotation? (b) Form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) and show the eigenvalues are not real. (c) One complex eigenvalue is \(\lambda=i\). Verify that \(v=(1,-i)\) (or an equivalent multiple) satisfies \(Av=\lambda v\).
C11. Dynamics connection. Suppose \(A\) has eigenpairs \((\lambda_1,v_1)\) and \((\lambda_2,v_2)\) with \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\), and \(x_0=c_1 v_1+c_2 v_2\) with \(c_1\neq 0\). In one or two sentences: what does \(A^k x_0\) look like for large \(k\)?


Least squares
C12. Consider the inconsistent system \[
\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}x
=
\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Here \(A\) is \(3\times 1\).)

Why is there no exact solution?
The least-squares \(\hat{x}\) minimizes \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert\). Compute \(\hat{x}\) using the normal equation \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (scalars here).
Compute the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) and \(\lVert r\rVert\).

C13. Same \(A\) and \(b\) as C12. Check that \(r\) is orthogonal to the column of \(A\).
C14. Data points \((0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,2)\) are to be fit by a line \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 t\) in the least-squares sense.

Write the matrix \(A\) and vector \(b\) in \(A\begin{bmatrix}\beta_0\\ \beta_1\end{bmatrix}\approx b\).
Form \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (you need not solve unless you want a check).



SVD concepts
C15. Suppose the singular values of a matrix are \(20,\ 5,\ 0.4,\ 0.01\).

Roughly how much of the “energy” (squared singular values) is in the top two components?
Why might a rank-\(2\) approximation be attractive for storage?
Name one thing a very low-rank model might miss.

C16. In the factorization \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\), which factor carries the singular values? What does “orthogonal factors” buy you conceptually (one sentence)?
C17. Software interpretation. A classmate reports eigenvalues \(1.00\) and \(0.02\) for a transition matrix and concludes “after many steps everything goes to zero.” What is the more careful reading in terms of dominant eigenbehavior?

title: Math 107 Final exam practice
text:
D. Mixed cumulative
Show reasoning. These mix units or require choosing a tool.
D1. Which tool? For each task, name a primary tool from: distance / cosine, span / independence / basis, \(Ax\) / transform, RREF / free variables, \(A^k\) / eigenvalues, least squares / residual, SVD / rank-\(k\), inverse / determinant.



Task
Tool




“Best fit when more equations than unknowns”



“Compress an image keeping the largest modes”



“All solutions of an underdetermined system”



“Will repeated application stretch one direction most?”



“Nearest catalog item to a query”



“Does this \(2\times 2\) squash area to zero?”




D2. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}4\\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Solve \(Ax=b\).
Find eigenvalues of \(A\) (hint: triangular).
Interpret \(A\) geometrically on the standard basis.

D3. A café stores each day as a \(3\)-vector (coffee, pastry, total) with total \(=\) coffee \(+\) pastry.

Write \(A\) so feature \(=Ax\) for \(x=(\text{coffee},\text{pastry})\).
What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)?
Why can redundant features hurt distance-based methods?

D4. Composition then eigen. Let \[
F=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] (reflection across the \(y\)-axis).

Compute \(F\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}\).
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(F\).
In one sentence: how do the eigen-directions relate to the geometry of reflection?

D5. Overdetermined fit vs exact solve. You have \(A\) that is \(100\times 3\) with independent columns, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{100}\).

Why is an exact solution of \(Ax=b\) unlikely?
What problem do you solve instead?
What does a small residual tell you? What does a large residual tell you?

D6. Dynamics + least squares flavor. States \(x_0=(1,0)\), \(x_1=(0.6,0.4)\), \(x_2=(0.52,0.48)\) come from \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with unknown \(2\times 2\) matrix \(A\). Explain in words how you could set up a least-squares problem to estimate the four entries of \(A\) from several observed pairs \((x_t,x_{t+1})\) (no need to solve a large system by hand).
D7. Null space and dependence. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix},
\] find nonzero \(x\) with \(Ax=0\), write the column dependence, compute \(\det A\), and say whether least squares for \(Ax\approx b\) has a unique \(\hat{x}\) for every \(b\in\mathbb{R}^2\).
D8. SVD decision. Two encodings of video frames: (i) store three frames separately and compress each with rank \(k\); (ii) store one frame plus two difference frames and compress those. In two sentences: what quantitative comparisons would you report (error, storage, runtime), and what might make (ii) win?
D9. Hand vs software. For each, say hand, software, or either and why in a few words:

\(2\times 2\) characteristic polynomial
eigenvalues of a \(50\times 50\) matrix
RREF of a \(3\times 4\) augmented matrix from class
rank-\(5\) approximation of a \(400\times 400\) image matrix
checking \(Av=\lambda v\) for a proposed pair

D10. Cumulative short proofs / reasons (2–4 sentences each).

If \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) with \(\lambda\neq 0\), explain why \(v\) cannot be in \(N(A)\).
If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<n\) for \(A\) that is \(m\times n\), explain why \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is not positive definite.
Why cosine similarity can prefer a different neighbor than Euclidean distance.

title: Math 107 Final exam practice
text:
Answers
Check only after a closed-book attempt. Update your definitions/formulas list for every miss.

A — Unit I
A1. \(c_1 a_1+\cdots+c_k a_k\) for scalars \(c_j\).
A2. \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=\sum_i a_i b_i\); orthogonal when the product is \(0\).
A3. Linear: \(f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)\) (equivalently \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\)). Affine allows a constant term: \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\).
A4. \(\lVert x\rVert=\sqrt{x^{\mathsf{T}}x}\); distance \(\lVert x-y\rVert\); cosine similarity \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b/(\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert)\).
A5. Independent spanning list; dimension \(=\) number of vectors in any basis.
A6. False — vectors can be close in position but point in very different directions (or vice versa for angle vs distance).
A7. (a) scalar (b) set of vectors (c) undefined — scalar plus vector (d) \(n\)-vector
A8. \(u+v=(3,3,1)\); \(2u-v=(6,-6,5)\); \(u^{\mathsf{T}}v=-6\).
A9. \(w=4a+1b\) (since \(4(1,0)+(1,1)=(5,1)\)).
A10. \(\lVert x\rVert=\sqrt{6}\); distance \(\sqrt{(3)^2+(-4)^2}=5\).
A11. \(\cos\theta=1/\sqrt{2}\); unit vector \((3/5,4/5)\).
A12. Affine — nonzero constant term (fails \(f(0)=0\) / superposition).
A13. Distances: to \(z_1\) is \(1\); to \(z_2\) is \(2\); to \(z_3\) is \(1\). Nearest: \(z_1\) or \(z_3\) (tie).
A14. Assign: \(x_1,x_2\to z_1\); \(x_3,x_4\to z_2\). Updated centers: \(z_1=(0,1)\), \(z_2=(6,1)\).
A15. Dependent: \((-2,-4)=-2(1,2)\).
A16. \((2,3,2)=2(1,0,1)+3(0,1,0)\) yes; \((1,1,0)\) no (any vector in \(V\) has equal first and third entries). \(\dim V=2\).


B — Unit II
B1. \(Ax=x_1 a_1+\cdots+x_n a_n\).
B2. \(b\in C(A)\).
B3. (i) inconsistent row \([0\cdots 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\); (ii) consistent, no free variables; (iii) consistent with a free variable.
B4. \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\); after \(k\) steps, \(x_k=A^k x_0\).
B5. \(C(A)=\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns}\}\); \(N(A)=\{x:Ax=0\}\); rank \(=\dim C(A)=\) number of pivots; \(\dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
B6. \(ad-bc\); \(|\det A|\) is the area scaling of the unit square.
B7. False — \(\det A=0\) means noninvertible.
B8. \(Ax=(-1,2)\); input \(\mathbb{R}^3\), output \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
B9. \(R e_1=(0,1)\), \(R e_2=(-1,0)\); \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation.
B10. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(b=(5,1)\); unique solution \(x=1\), \(y=2\).
B11. Pivots \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\); \(x=(3-2t,\ 1+t,\ t)\).
B12. \(x_1=(0.5,0.5)\); \(x_2=(0.5,0.5)\); \(x_3=A^3 x_0\).
B13. \(AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}\), \(BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}\); not equal; \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
B14. Inverse \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Second matrix not invertible: \(\det=0\); columns dependent / nontrivial null space.
B15. Rank \(2\); free \(x_2=s\), \(x_4=t\); \[
x=s\begin{bmatrix}-2\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-3\\ 0\\ 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix};
\] \(\dim N(A)=2\); \(2+2=4\).
B16. \(10\); \(-30\).
B17. Outer-product-first builds an \(n\times n\) matrix; \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) only needs a dot product then a scale — much cheaper.


C — Since Midterm 2
C1. \(Av=\lambda v\) with \(v\neq 0\).
C2. \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).
C3. Point \((a,b)\) in the plane; sum \(4+i\); product \((1)(3)+(1)(-i)+(2i)(3)+(2i)(-i)=3-i+6i-2i^2=5+5i\).
C4. Minimize \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert\) over \(x\); residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) (or \(Ax-b\) with sign convention stated).
C5. Keeps the \(k\) largest singular components; discards the rest (smaller modes / noise / fine detail).
C6. False — least squares is exactly for inconsistent / overdetermined cases.
C7. False — \(90^\circ\) rotation has no real eigenvector (eigenvalues \(\pm i\)).
C8. \(Av=(0,3)=3v\), so \(\lambda=3\).
C9. \(A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}4-\lambda&1\\ 2&3-\lambda\end{bmatrix}\); \(\det=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0\); \(\lambda=5,2\). For \(\lambda=5\): \((A-5I)v=0\) gives \(\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\ 2&-2\end{bmatrix}v=0\), so \(v=(1,1)\) (or multiple).
C10. (a) \((0,1)\) and \((-1,0)\); yes, \(90^\circ\) CCW rotation. (b) \(\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+1=0\), so \(\lambda=\pm i\). (c) \(Av=(i,1)\) and \(i v=(i,-i^2)=(i,1)\); match.
C11. \(A^k x_0=c_1\lambda_1^k v_1+c_2\lambda_2^k v_2\) is dominated by the \(\lambda_1^k v_1\) term (direction of \(v_1\), scaled by \(\lambda_1^k\)).
C12. (a) \(b\) not a multiple of \((1,1,1)\) (entries not equal). (b) \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A=3\), \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b=5\), so \(\hat{x}=5/3\). (c) \(A\hat{x}=(5/3,5/3,5/3)\); \(r=(-2/3,1/3,1/3)\); \(\lVert r\rVert=\sqrt{2/3}=\sqrt{6}/3\).
C13. Column is \((1,1,1)\); \(r^{\mathsf{T}}(1,1,1)=-2/3+1/3+1/3=0\).
C14. (a) \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
\] (b) \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A=\begin{bmatrix}3&3\\ 3&5\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\ 6\end{bmatrix}\).
C15. (a) Energy \(\propto 20^2+5^2+0.4^2+0.01^2=400+25+0.16+0.0001\); top two are \(425/425.16\approx 99.96\%\). (b) Store two singular triples / factors instead of the full matrix. (c) Fine detail, small features, or structured residuals in the discarded modes.
C16. \(\Sigma\) (diagonal of singular values). Orthogonal \(U,V\) give orthonormal bases for row/column spaces / preserve norms in those coordinates.
C17. The mode with \(|\lambda|\approx 1\) dominates; the state tends toward that eigen-direction (not necessarily to zero). The \(0.02\) mode dies out.


D — Mixed
D1. Least squares / residual; SVD / rank-\(k\); RREF / free variables; \(A^k\) / eigenvalues; distance / cosine; inverse / determinant.
D2. (a) \(x_2=2\), \(x_1=2\). (b) Both eigenvalues \(1\) (diagonal of triangular matrix). (c) \(e_1\mapsto e_1\), \(e_2\mapsto(1,1)\) — shear.
D3. (a) \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) Rank \(2\). (c) Redundant coordinate double-counts / distorts distances.
D4. (a) \((-1,2)\). (b) Eigenvalues \(\pm 1\): e.g. \(\lambda=1\) with \((0,1)\) (fixed \(y\)-axis); \(\lambda=-1\) with \((1,0)\) (reversed \(x\)-axis). (c) Eigen-directions are the axis that stays put and the axis that flips.
D5. (a) \(b\) almost surely not in the \(3\)-dimensional column space. (b) \(\min_x\lVert Ax-b\rVert\). (c) Small residual: data nearly consistent with the model; large residual: model misspecification or large noise / wrong features.
D6. Each pair gives \(x_{t+1}\approx A x_t\), i.e. two linear equations in the four unknown entries of \(A\). Stack many timesteps into one big overdetermined system \(M a \approx y\) for the vectorized entries \(a\) of \(A\), then solve in the least-squares sense.
D7. e.g. \(x=(2,-1)\); \(2c_1-c_2=0\); \(\det A=0\); least-squares \(\hat{x}\) is not unique for every \(b\) (columns dependent \(\Rightarrow A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) singular; infinitely many minimizers when any exist).
D8. Report reconstruction error (e.g. RMS / Frobenius), storage for the kept factors, and factorization / reconstruction time. Differences are often more compressible (singular values decay faster), so (ii) can win on storage/error for the same \(k\).
D9. (a) hand (or either); (b) software; (c) hand / either; (d) software; (e) either (hand for tiny; software numerically).
D10. (a) \(Av=\lambda v\neq 0\), so \(v\notin N(A)\). (b) Independent columns fail \(\Rightarrow\) nonzero \(x\) with \(Ax=0\Rightarrow x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=0\) with \(x\neq 0\), so not positive definite. (c) Distance cares about position; cosine cares about direction — a long vector nearly parallel to the query can beat a closer but angled neighbor under cosine, and vice versa under distance.

Unit III — Since Midterm 2 (Lectures 35–40)

Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair \((A,v,\lambda)\) by checking \(Av=\lambda v\).
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.



Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors (including simple complex cases at the course’s level).
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.



Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way? (+ Lab 5 / Quiz 10)

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors with software and verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\).
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain growth, decay, or approach to a direction.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation / oscillation behavior.
Observe orthogonal eigenvectors for a symmetric example when it appears.
Connect eigen-language back to earlier dynamical simulations.



Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) as the closest attainable vector in \(C(A)\).
Interpret the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.



Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness (+ Lab 6)

Compute a least-squares solution with software (and check a tiny case by hand when asked).
Interpret residuals and RMS error in context.
Check that the residual is orthogonal to the columns of \(A\) (normal equations idea).
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and positive definite when \(A\) has independent columns.
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful, not only report coefficients.



Lecture 40 — SVD, low-rank approximation, and capstone launch

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually (orthogonal factors + singular values).
Explain what a rank-\(k\) approximation keeps and what it discards.
Compare singular-value decay qualitatively for different data matrices.
Relate reconstruction error and storage to the choice of rank \(k\).
State a practical limitation of a low-rank model (what structure it may miss).

title: Midterm 1 study guide

Learning outcomes (Lectures 01–14)

Lecture 01 — Vectors as representations

Identify objects that can be represented as vectors.
Interpret vector entries, units, and indexing in context.
Distinguish scalars from vectors.
Translate a small data, position, signal, or measurement problem into vector form.



Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry

Add, subtract, and scale vectors.
Interpret those operations geometrically.
Plot vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and recognize corresponding operations in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
Check whether an answer has sensible dimensions and units.



Lecture 03 — Linear combinations (+ Lab 0)

Form and interpret linear combinations.
Explain the meaning of coefficients in context.
Enter, index, and modify vectors in Octave or Python.
Perform vector arithmetic and create a basic plot.
Modify supplied code and explain its output or error message.



Lecture 04 — Inner product

Compute a dot product.
Interpret it as a weighted sum.
Interpret its sign and magnitude as alignment.
Recognize orthogonal vectors from a zero dot product.



Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions

Distinguish linear from affine functions in examples.
Test superposition numerically on simple functions.
Construct a function \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) for a contextual quantity.
Evaluate a model by hand and computationally.



Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications

Model a score, cost, prediction, or aggregate quantity.
Interpret model coefficients and intercepts.
Compare outputs from competing models.
State a reasonable limitation or assumption of a linear model.



Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation

Compute vector norms and distances.
Interpret norm and distance geometrically and contextually.
Relate norm to RMS and, where appropriate, variation around an average.
Use software to calculate distances in dimensions too large for hand computation.



Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity

Compute cosine similarity or an angle between vectors.
Distinguish closeness in position from similarity in direction.
Choose an appropriate similarity measure for a stated purpose.
Explain why normalization may change a comparison.



Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors

Formulate a nearest-neighbor question using vectors.
Find a nearest neighbor in a small dataset by hand.
Explain how feature scale can affect the answer.
Justify a choice of distance or similarity measure.



Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means

Explain the goal of clustering.
Compute one assignment/update iteration of \(k\)-means.
Interpret a centroid as a vector.
Recognize that clustering output depends on representation, scaling, and initialization.



Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy

Recognize simple dependent and independent collections.
Construct a dependence relationship.
Interpret dependence as redundant information.
Explain why redundancy matters in data, measurement, and computation.



Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces

Define span using linear combinations.
Determine whether a vector lies in a simple span.
Interpret spans geometrically as lines, planes, or higher-dimensional collections.
Recognize basic subspaces and distinguish them from shifted lines or planes.



Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors

Explain what a basis accomplishes.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use linear combination, span, subspace, independence, basis, and dimension accurately.
Recognize an orthonormal collection.
Explain why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
A. Definitions and meaning
Write a short precise answer (one or two sentences, or a formula). No long essays.
A1. What does it mean to say that \(A\) is an \(m\times n\) matrix? What size is each column of \(A\)?
A2. Give the column view formula for \(Ax\) when \(A\) has columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).
A3. In one sentence: what does it mean to interpret \(A\) as a transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^m\)?
A4. Name three structured matrix types from class (beyond “square”) and one practical consequence of structure for at least one of them.
A5. Translate “\(Ax=b\) has a solution” into a statement about the column space of \(A\).
A6. What is reduced row echelon form (RREF)? What are pivot and free variables?
A7. When does \(Ax=b\) have (i) no solution, (ii) a unique solution, (iii) infinitely many solutions? Answer in terms of RREF / consistency / free variables for a square or rectangular system.
A8. Write the model for a linear dynamical system used in class. What do the state \(x_t\) and matrix \(A\) represent?
A9. When is the product \(AB\) defined? What are the dimensions of \(AB\) if \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\)?
A10. Why is matrix multiplication not generally commutative? Give a one-line reason (sizes or a counterexample idea).
A11. How does \(A^k x\) relate to the dynamical system \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\)?
A12. What does it mean for \(A\) to be invertible? How does invertibility relate to uniqueness of solutions of \(Ax=b\)?
A13. Why is solving \(Ax=b\) generally preferable to forming \(A^{-1}\) and computing \(A^{-1}b\)?
A14. Define the column space \(C(A)\) and the null space \(N(A)\).
A15. Define \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\). How does rank relate to \(\dim C(A)\) and \(\dim N(A)\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix?
A16. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{bmatrix}\), write \(\det A\). What does \(|\det A|\) mean geometrically for the image of the unit square?
A17. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(\det A=0\), then \(A\) is invertible.”
A18. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(AB=I\), then \(BA\) must also equal \(I\) for square \(A,B\) of the same size.” (You may assume the course’s usual finite-dimensional setting.)
A19. Light review (Quiz 5): What is a basis of a subspace \(V\)? What is \(\dim V\)?
A20. For each expression, say whether the result is a scalar, an \(n\)-vector, an \(m\times n\) matrix, a set of vectors, or undefined (brief reason if undefined). Assume sizes make sense unless noted.

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
B. Computational
Show your work for each calculation.

Matrices, \(Ax\), and transforms
B1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&2\\ 0&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) using the column-combination view.
B2. Same \(A\) as B1. What are the input and output dimensions of the map \(x\mapsto Ax\)?
B3. Let \[
R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(R\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(R\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\). Describe the geometric effect of \(R\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
B4. Let \[
S=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(S\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(S\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\). What kind of transform is this (scaling / reflection / shear / rotation)?
B5. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A+B\), \(2A\), and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\).
B6. Is \[
T=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}
\] symmetric? Triangular? Diagonal?


Systems, elimination, RREF
B7. Write the linear system \[
\begin{aligned}
x+2y&=5,\\
3x-y&=1
\end{aligned}
\] as \(Ax=b\). Give \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\).
B8. Solve the system in B7 by hand (elimination or substitution). How many solutions?
B9. The augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\) row-reduces to \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Identify pivot variables and free variables. Write the general solution parametrically.
B10. Same RREF idea, but the last row is \([0\ 0\ 0\ |\ 4]\). How many solutions? Why?
B11. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 3 \\
2 & 4 & | & 6
\end{bmatrix}
\] to RREF. Describe the solution set of the corresponding system.
B12. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 7\end{bmatrix},
\] is \(b\) in \(C(A)\)? Brief reason (no need for full RREF if you see the issue quickly).


Dynamics
B13. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix},\quad
x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and \(x_2=Ax_1\).
B14. A two-state system has transition matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] (urban/rural fractions as in lecture). If \(x_0=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and interpret the entries.
B15. For the system \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with the \(A\) from B13, express \(x_3\) in terms of \(A\) and \(x_0\) using a matrix power (do not expand the power by hand unless you want to check).


Matrix products, powers, cost
B16. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(AB\) and \(BA\). Are they equal?
B17. With \(A\) from B16, compute \(A^2\).
B18. Dimensions: \(A\) is \(4\times 3\), \(B\) is \(3\times 2\), \(C\) is \(2\times 5\). Is \((AB)C\) defined? What size is it? Is \(A(BC)\) defined?
B19. Suppose \(a\) is a \(1000\)-vector, \(b\) is a \(1000\)-vector, and \(c\) is a \(1000\)-vector. Compare forming \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) versus \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) in words: which forms a huge intermediate matrix, and which is cheaper?
B20. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A^2\) and \(A^3\). Guess a formula for \(A^k\).


Inverses
B21. Find the inverse of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] (if it exists) by finding a matrix \(B\) with \(AB=I\).
B22. Is \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}
\] invertible? Give two different reasons (e.g. determinant, dependent columns, or null space).
B23. Solve \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 2\end{bmatrix}
\] without forming an inverse explicitly (back substitution / elimination is fine).


Rank, column space, null space
B24. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\). Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Is \(b=(1,3,0)\) in \(C(A)\)?
B25. Same \(A\) as B24. Find \(N(A)\) (solve \(Ax=0\)). Give a basis for \(N(A)\), or state that only \(0\) is in the null space.
B26. The RREF of a \(3\times 4\) matrix \(A\) is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)? Which original columns form a basis for \(C(A)\) (pivot columns)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\).
B27. For the matrix in B26, what is \(\dim N(A)\)? Check that \(\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim N(A)=n\).


Determinants
B28. Compute \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]
B29. Compute \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\ 0&-3&4\\ 0&0&5\end{bmatrix}.
\]
B30. The linear map given by \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix}\) sends the unit square to a rectangle. What is the area of that rectangle? How does this relate to \(\det A\)?
B31. Does \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}=0
\] tell you that the columns are dependent? That \(A\) is noninvertible? That \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\)?

C. Applied / harder
Show reasoning. These mix ideas or need a careful choice of tool.
C1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad

\]

Solve \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(A\) as a transformation of \(\mathbb{R}^2\): what does it do to the standard basis vectors?

C2. A café stores each day as a \(3\)-vector (coffee sold, pastry sold, total items), where total \(=\) coffee \(+\) pastry.

Write a matrix \(A\) (or describe its columns) so that “feature vector” \(=Ax\) for an underlying \(2\)-vector \(x=(\text{coffee},\text{pastry})\).

C3. Dynamics and products. Let \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with \[

In one sentence: what long-run behavior do you see?

C4. Composition. A point is first reflected across the \(y\)-axis by \[

text:
Answers
Check only after a closed-book attempt. Update your definitions/formulas list for every miss.

A — Definitions (key points)
A1. \(A\) has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns; each column is an \(m\)-vector.
A2. \(Ax=x_1 a_1+\cdots+x_n a_n\).
A3. \(A\) maps each input \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) to the output \(Ax\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
A4. e.g. identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, sparse, zero — sparse saves storage/ops; triangular makes determinants/back-substitution easy; etc.
A5. \(b\in C(A)\) (equivalently: \(b\) is a linear combination of the columns).
A6. RREF is a row-echelon form with pivots \(1\) and zeros above/below pivots. Pivot variables correspond to pivot columns; free variables are the non-pivot unknowns.
A7. (i) inconsistent row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\); (ii) consistent and no free variables; (iii) consistent with at least one free variable.
A8. \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\); \(x_t\) is the state, \(A\) is the transition / update matrix.
A9. Inner dimensions match (\(A\)’s columns \(=\) \(B\)’s rows); \(AB\) is \(m\times p\).
A10. Order matters: \(AB\) and \(BA\) need not both be defined, and even when both are, they need not be equal.
A11. \(x_k=A^k x_0\) (after \(k\) steps).
A12. There exists \(A^{-1}\) with \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\). For square \(A\), invertible iff \(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\).
A13. Forming \(A^{-1}\) is more work / less stable; solving the system directly is the standard approach.
A14. \(C(A)=\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\); \(N(A)=\{x:Ax=0\}\).
A15. Rank \(=\) dimension of the column space (\(=\) number of pivots). For \(m\times n\) matrix: \(\dim C(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and \(\dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
A16. \(ad-bc\); absolute value \(=\) area scaling factor for the unit square (signed area accounts for orientation).
A17. False — \(\det A=0\) means noninvertible.
A18. True (in this course’s finite-dimensional square-matrix setting): a one-sided inverse is a two-sided inverse.
A19. Independent spanning list; dimension \(=\) number of vectors in any basis.
A20. (a) \(m\)-vector (b) \(m\times n\) matrix (c) undefined — inner dimensions \(3\neq 2\) (d) \(n\times m\) matrix (e) scalar (f) undefined — singular, no inverse (g) set of vectors (h) set of vectors (i) scalar (nonnegative integer) (j) undefined — \(A\) is not square / \(A A\) sizes fail (k) \(2\)-vector (l) \(m\)-vector that is \(0\) when consistent (here the zero vector)


B — Easy computations
B1. \(Ax=2\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+1\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 3\end{bmatrix}+(-1)\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}\).
B2. Input \(\mathbb{R}^3\), output \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
B3. \(R e_1=(0,1)\), \(R e_2=(-1,0)\); \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation.
B4. \(S e_1=(1,0)\), \(S e_2=(2,1)\); shear (horizontal shear).
B5. \(A+B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}\); \(2A=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\ 0&6\end{bmatrix}\); \(A^{\mathsf{T}}=A\) (already symmetric diagonal).
B6. Symmetric: yes. Triangular: no. Diagonal: no.
B7. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(x=\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}\), \(b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\).
B8. Unique solution: e.g. \(x=1\), \(y=2\) (check: \(1+4=5\), \(3-2=1\)).
B9. Pivots \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). General: \(x=(3-2t,\ 1+t,\ t)\).
B10. No solutions — inconsistent (\(0=4\)).
B11. RREF \(\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}\); infinitely many: \(x_1=3-2t\), \(x_2=t\).
B12. No — second row of \(A\) is \(2\times\) first, but \(7\neq 2\cdot 3\).
B13. \(x_1=(0.5,0.5)\); \(x_2=(0.5,0.5)\).
B14. \(x_1=(0.9\cdot 0.6+0.2\cdot 0.4,\ 0.1\cdot 0.6+0.8\cdot 0.4)=(0.62,0.38)\); urban / rural fractions tomorrow.
B15. \(x_3=A^3 x_0\).
B16. \(AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}\), \(BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}\); not equal.
B17. \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
B18. Yes, size \(4\times 5\); yes, \(A(BC)\) also \(4\times 5\).
B19. \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) builds a \(1000\times 1000\) matrix; \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) only needs a dot product then a scale — much cheaper.
B20. \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^3=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\); \(A^k=\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
B21. \(B=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\) (check \(AB=I\)).
B22. Not invertible: \(\det=0\); columns dependent (\(c_2=2c_1\)); nontrivial null space, e.g. \((2,-1)\).
B23. From second row \(x_2=2\); first row \(x_1+x_2=3\) so \(x_1=1\).
B24. \(C(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(0,0,1)\}=\{(x,2x,z)\}\). \((1,2,3)\): yes; \((1,3,0)\): no (middle entry must be twice the first).
B25. \(Ax=0\) forces \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=0\); \(N(A)=\{0\}\) (two pivot columns; only the trivial null vector).
B26. Rank \(2\); pivot columns 1 and 3 of the original \(A\). Free variables \(x_2=s\), \(x_4=t\). From RREF: \(x_1+2s+3t=0\), \(x_3-t=0\), so \[
x=s\begin{bmatrix}-2\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-3\\ 0\\ 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Basis for \(N(A)\): those two vectors.
B27. \(\dim N(A)=2\); \(2+2=4=n\).
B28. \(12-2=10\).
B29. Product of diagonal: \(2\cdot(-3)\cdot 5=-30\).
B30. Area \(6\); equals \(|\det A|=6\).
B31. Yes; yes; yes (column space is not all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)).


C — Harder
C1. (a) \(x_2=2\), \(x_1=2\). (b) \(e_1\mapsto e_1\), \(e_2\mapsto(1,1)\) — shear. (c) Square invertible matrix / unique RREF pivots in both columns / \(\det A=1\neq 0\).
C2. (a) e.g. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) Yes — third row \(=\) sum of first two; \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\). (c) Redundant feature double-counts / distorts distance-based methods.
C3. (a) \(x_1=(1,0)\), \(x_2=(0,0)\), \(x_3=(0,0)\). (b) \(A^2=0\), so \(x_2=A^2 x_0=0\). (c) Dies to zero in two steps.
C4. (a) \(RF\). (b) \(RF=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ -1&0\end{bmatrix}\); \((RF)(1,0)=(0,-1)\).
C5. (a) \(n\times n\). (b) Scalar \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c\), then multiply by \(a\). (c) \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) — avoids the huge matrix.
C6. (a) Column 2 \(=2\times\) column 1. (b) \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\) (e.g. columns 1 and 3 are independent; column 2 is redundant). (c) \(b=(0,0,0)\) always solvable; \(b=(3,6,1)\) is column 3, so solvable; \(b=(1,0,0)\) not in \(C(A)\) (any combination has second entry equal to twice the first).
C7. e.g. \(x=(2,-1)\); \(2c_1-c_2=0\).
C8. (i) \(8\), invertible; (ii) \(0\), not invertible; (iii) \(-15\), invertible.
C9. Determinant; column space / \(Ax=b\); RREF / free variables; inverse; dynamical iteration \(A^k x\); matrix product / composition; computational reordering; rank / independent columns.
C10. Free variable \(x_3=t\); solution \(x=(-2t,\ t,\ t)\), not only zero.
C11. (a) Images \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\); parallelogram is the unit-area shear of the square. (b) \(\det A=1\); area \(1\). (c) Yes invertible — parallelogram has positive area / does not collapse.
C12. (a) Basis e.g. \(\{(1,0,1)\}\); \(\dim=1\). (b) \((1,0,1)\) yes; \((1,1,1)\) no (middle entry). (c) \(x_1+2x_2+3x_3=0\); basis e.g. \(\{(-2,1,0),(-3,0,1)\}\).
C13. (a) \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\ 0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix}\) (columns: where each room’s students go — column 1 from Room 1, column 2 from Room 2). (b) \(x_1=(80,20)\). (c) Yes — total \(100\) preserved (columns sum to \(1\)).

title: Midterm 2 study guide
text:
Learning outcomes (Lectures 18–32)

Light review — Quiz 5 / basis (Lecture 14)

Explain what a basis accomplishes and what dimension means.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use span, independence, basis, and dimension accurately when they reappear with matrices (column space, null space, rank).



Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects

Identify matrix dimensions, rows, columns, and entries.
Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.



Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.



Lecture 20 — Transforming space (+ Lab 3)

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.



Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)

Translate equations or contextual constraints into \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) belongs to the span of the columns of \(A\).
Classify systems as square, underdetermined, or overdetermined.
Anticipate circumstances producing zero, one, or many solutions.



Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination

Perform elementary row operations.
Reduce a small augmented matrix to echelon form.
Solve a small system using back substitution.
Explain why row operations preserve the solution set.



Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify with a residual.



Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.



Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.



Lecture 26 — Predict a system through time (+ Lab 4)

Implement a linear dynamical model.
Write or complete a short iterative calculation.
Validate the first steps by hand.
Compare results under altered parameters or initial states.
Record an unexplained long-run pattern for later investigation (eigenvalues come later).



Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions.
Compute a small matrix product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations.
Explain why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.



Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers

Combine multistage processes using a matrix product.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.
Interpret selected entries of a matrix product or power.
Recognize how network and transition information accumulates through powers.



Lecture 29 — Computational cost

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.



Lecture 30 — Inverses and solving

Interpret an inverse as undoing a transformation.
Determine whether a simple matrix is invertible.
Connect invertibility to uniqueness of \(Ax=b\).
Explain why solving \(Ax=b\) is generally preferable computationally to explicitly calculating \(A^{-1}\).



Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.
Connect rank to consistency, independence, and dimension.
Use subspace, basis, dimension, rank, column space, and null space correctly.



Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation (preview only).

title: Lab 4 — Predict a System Through Time
text:
Exercises
Pick Octave or Python for the term. Use column vectors for states.
E1. Hand-check one step. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1000\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) on paper.
Check with code.
Compute \(x_2\) on paper; check with one more A*x / A @ x.

Octave: A = [0.9 0.2; 0.1 0.8]; x = [1000; 0]; x = A*x
Python: A = np.array([[0.9, 0.2], [0.1, 0.8]]); x = np.array([1000., 0.]); x = A @ x
Expected: \(x_1=(900,100)\); \(x_2=(830,170)\).
E2. Iterate. Starting from the same \(A\) and \(x_0\) as E1, write a loop that applies \(A\) twenty times. Print (or store) \(x_5\) and \(x_{20}\).
Octave sketch:
A = [0.9 0.2; 0.1 0.8];
x = [1000; 0];
for t = 1:20
  x = A*x;
  if t == 5 || t == 20
    disp(x')
  end
end
Python sketch:
A = np.array([[0.9, 0.2], [0.1, 0.8]])
x = np.array([1000., 0.])
for t in range(1, 21):
    x = A @ x
    if t in (5, 20):
        print(t, x)
Expected (rounded): \(x_5\approx(722.7,\,277.3)\); \(x_{20}\approx(666.9,\,333.1)\). (Exact fractions not required — match to about \(1\) person.)
E3. Plot. Modify E2 to store both components at every time \(t=0,\ldots,20\), then plot each component versus \(t\). Do the curves look like growth, decay, oscillation, or stabilization?
Expected answer: stabilization (approach a steady mix near two-thirds / one-third); no oscillation.
E4. What-if parameter. Replace \(A\) by \[
A_{\mathrm{new}}=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.2\\ 0.3&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] (same \(x_0=(1000,0)\)). Recompute \(x_1\) by hand and with code, then simulate to \(t=20\). In one sentence: how does the long-run on-campus share compare to E2?
Expected: \(x_1=(700,300)\); by \(t=20\) the first component is near \(400\) (lower on-campus share than E2’s \(\sim 667\)).
E5. Mystery log (save for Week 13). Let \[
B=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\ 0&0.5\end{bmatrix}.
\] Simulate from \(x_0=(1,0)\) and from \(y_0=(0,1)\) for about \(15\) steps each (print a few values or sketch).

Describe the two long-run behaviors in plain language.
On the ticket, write one question you cannot yet answer with a formula (eigenvalue theory is off-limits today).

Expected: from \((1,0)\) the state grows; from \((0,1)\) it decays toward \(0\). Sample mystery: “Why does the direction of the start decide growth vs decay?”
E6 (stretch). Oscillation. Let \(C=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(1,0)\). Compute \(x_1,\ldots,x_4\) by hand or code. What geometric map is \(C\)? Does \(\|x_t\|\) change?
Expected: \(x_1=(0,1)\), \(x_2=(-1,0)\), \(x_3=(0,-1)\), \(x_4=(1,0)\); \(90^\circ\) CCW rotation; norm stays \(1\).

title: Lab 5 — Why Did the System Behave That Way?
text:
Exercises
Pick Octave or Python for the term.
E1. Lab 4 mystery explained. Let \[
B=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Use software to find eigenpairs of \(B\).
Verify \(Bv=\lambda v\) for each pair (hand or code).
In one sentence: why does \(x_0=(1,0)\) grow while \(y_0=(0,1)\) decays?

E2. Verify a nondiagonal matrix. Let \[

\] (from Lab 4 E1).

Compute eigenpairs with software.
For each pair, print \(\|Av-\lambda v\|\) (or the residual vector). Accept “near zero.”
Which eigenvalue has larger absolute value? Predict the long-run direction of \(A^t x_0\) for a generic \(x_0\).

Expected: eigenvalues \(1\) and \(0.7\) (exactly, up to rounding); dominant \(\lambda=1\) with eigenvector along \((2,1)\) (or parallel). Stabilization toward that mix matches Lab 4.
E3. Simulate and explain. Same \(A\) as E2, \(x_0=(1000,0)\). Run about \(20\) steps (reuse Lab 4 code). Using E2’s eigenpairs, explain in 2–3 sentences why the state approaches a steady mix rather than blowing up or oscillating.
Expected: both \(|\lambda|\le 1\); the \(\lambda=1\) mode persists and the \(|\lambda|=0.7\) mode decays, so \(x_t\) settles along the \(\lambda=1\) eigenvector.
E4. Complex / oscillation. Let \[
R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Software eigenvalues (expect near \(\pm i\)).
Compute \(x_0=(1,0)\), \(x_1=Rx_0\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), \(x_4\) by hand or code.
In one sentence: how do complex eigenvalues relate to the cycling you see?

Expected: \(\lambda=\pm i\); states cycle every \(4\) steps on the unit circle; complex eigenvalues encode pure rotation / oscillation (no real persistent direction).
E5. Symmetric / normal-mode peek. Let \[
S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}
\] (symmetric; same as the demo).

Get both eigenvectors \(v_1,v_2\) from software.
Compute \(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2\). Are they orthogonal (up to rounding)?
Normal modes (application/demo): for a symmetric vibration-style matrix, orthogonal eigenvectors are the independent “shapes” that stay aligned under \(S\). No differential-equation derivation required — just observe the orthogonality.

Expected: \(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2\approx 0\); yes, orthogonal.
E6 (stretch). Dominant growth. Let \(C=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(1,1)\). Find eigenpairs; identify the dominant \(|\lambda|\); simulate to \(t=15\) and comment whether \(\|x_t\|\) grows roughly like \(|\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}|^t\).

Exercises
Pick Octave or Python for the term. Use column vectors for \(b\) and \(\hat{x}\).
E1. Impossible by hand, possible by least squares. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Argue briefly that \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution (two equations already force a third that fails).
Compute \(\hat{x}\) with A\b / lstsq.
Report \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\), \(r=b-\hat{b}\), and \(\|r\|\).

Expected (rounded): \(\hat{x}\approx(1.167,\,0.500)\); \(\|r\|\approx 0.408\).
E2. Real-ish line fit. Five evening study-hour totals \(t=1,\ldots,5\) (hours) and self-reported focus scores \(b\) (0–10): \[
b=(3.0,\,4.5,\,4.0,\,6.5,\,7.0).
\] Use the model \(b\approx x_1 + x_2 t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\\1&5
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Compute \(\hat{x}\).
Compute \(\hat{b}\), \(r\), and \(\mathrm{RMS}=\|r\|/\sqrt{5}\).
In one sentence: on a 0–10 focus scale, is this RMS small enough to call the line useful?

Expected: \(\hat{x}=(2,\,1)\) (exact from normal equations); RMS \(=\sqrt{3/10}\approx 0.548\).
E3. Plot. Using the E2 data, plot observed \(b\) vs \(t\) as markers and fitted \(\hat{b}\) as a line (same axes). Label axes. Does the line capture the overall trend despite the dip at \(t=3\)?
Expected answer: yes — upward trend; \(t=3\) sits below the line (visible residual).
E4. Orthogonality. For your E2 fit, compute \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\). How close to \((0,0)\) is it? Why should it be near zero?
Expected: entries on the order of \(10^{-15}\) (roundoff); residual \(\perp C(A)\) at a least-squares solution.
E5. Usefulness, not just coefficients. A classmate reports only “\(\hat{x}=(2,\,1)\)” with no plot and no RMS.

What two checks would you still demand?
Suppose instead RMS \(=3.5\) on the same 0–10 scale. Useful linear model? Why or why not?

Expected: (a) plot / residual look + RMS (or \(\|r\|\)) in context; (b) not useful — typical error is huge relative to the score scale.
E6 (stretch). PSD check. Form \(P=A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) for the E2 matrix \(A\). Verify \(P^{\mathsf{T}}=P\) and, for \(x=(1,-1)\), that \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px=\|Ax\|^2\ge 0\). Are the columns of \(A\) independent? Is \(P\) positive definite?
Expected: yes independent (Vandermonde-style line model); \(P\) PD, so \(\hat{x}\) unique.

title: Micro-lab — Computational cost
text:
Exercises
Pick Octave or Python for the term. Use the same random \(a,b,c\) when comparing two orders for a fixed \(n\).
E1. Tiny hand check. With \(a=(1,0,-1)\), \(b=(2,1,0)\), \(c=(1,1,1)\), compute by hand (or tiny code) both \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\).
Expected answer: both equal \((3,0,-3)\) (since \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c=3\)).
E2. Storage. For general \(n\), how many entries are stored in the intermediate \(M=ab^{\mathsf{T}}\)? How many numbers is the intermediate scalar \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\)? For \(n=2000\), write both counts.
Expected answer: \(n^2\) vs \(1\); for \(n=2000\): \(4{,}000{,}000\) vs \(1\).
E3. Agree for larger \(n\). Generate random \(n\)-vectors with \(n=500\). Compute \[
y_1=(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c,\qquad y_2=a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)
\] and report a measure of agreement (e.g. norm(y1-y2) / np.linalg.norm(y1-y2)).
Octave:
n = 500;
a = randn(n,1); b = randn(n,1); c = randn(n,1);
y1 = (a*b')*c;
y2 = a*(b'*c);
norm(y1-y2)
Python:
import numpy as np
n = 500
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.standard_normal(n); b = rng.standard_normal(n); c = rng.standard_normal(n)
y1 = np.outer(a, b) @ c
y2 = a * (b @ c)
print(np.linalg.norm(y1 - y2))
Expected output: a tiny number (order \(10^{-10}\) or smaller — floating-point noise, not a modeling error).
E4. Time both orders. For \(n=200\), \(n=1000\), and \(n=3000\) (skip \(3000\) on a slow machine if needed), time Order 1 (a*b')*c / np.outer(a,b)@c and Order 2 a*(b'*c) / a*(b@c). Record times on the ticket.
Octave pattern:
n = 1000;
a = randn(n,1); b = randn(n,1); c = randn(n,1);
tic; y1 = (a*b')*c; t1 = toc;
tic; y2 = a*(b'*c); t2 = toc;
t1, t2
Python pattern:
import numpy as np, time
n = 1000
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
a = rng.standard_normal(n); b = rng.standard_normal(n); c = rng.standard_normal(n)
t0 = time.perf_counter(); y1 = np.outer(a, b) @ c; t1 = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); y2 = a * (b @ c); t2 = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(t1, t2)
Expected: Order 2 much faster; the gap grows with \(n\). Absolute times vary by machine — report yours.
E5. Justify. In 2–3 sentences on the ticket: which order would you use for \(n=10^4\), and what two quantitative observations (storage count + timing trend) support that choice?
Expected answer (idea): scalar-first — stores \(1\) intermediate vs \(10^8\) matrix entries; timings show Order 1 growing far faster (roughly with \(n^2\)).

text:

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Warm-up
Rewrite the system \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - 2x_2 &= 3 \\
2x_1 + x_2 &= 1
\end{aligned}
\] as \(Ax=b\). What are \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\)? Is \(b\) in the span of the columns of \(A\)? (You may decide by solving or by a short span argument.)

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Fill in
A linear system with \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns can be written \(Ax=b\), where \(A\) is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\), \(x\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector, and \(b\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector.
Column view. Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\)? Equivalently: does \(b\) lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\)?
Shape vocabulary (compare \(m\) equations to \(n\) unknowns):








Name
Relation
Typical intuition




Square
\(m=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often one solution, but not always


Overdetermined
\(m>\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (too many constraints)


Underdetermined
\(m<\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (free variables)



These are tendencies, not guarantees: a square system can be inconsistent or have infinitely many solutions; an overdetermined system can still be consistent.
Possible outcomes for \(Ax=b\):

No solution — \(b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) the column space.
Unique solution — \(b\) is in the column space in exactly \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) way.
Infinitely many solutions — \(b\) is in the column space in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) ways (free parameters).

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Worked in class
W1. Matrix form. Three unknowns \(x_1,x_2,x_3\): \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &= 4 \\
x_2 - x_3 &= 1 \\
2x_1 + x_3 &= 3.
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\). Square / over / under?
W2. Span interpretation. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\end{bmatrix},\quad
c=\begin{bmatrix}3\\5\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Are the columns of \(A\) independent? Describe \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns}\}\). (b) Does \(Ax=b\) have a solution? Infinitely many? (c) Does \(Ax=c\) have a solution?
W3. Context → \(Ax=b\). A café sells tea (\(\$2\)) and coffee (\(\$3\)). On Monday they sold \(x_1\) teas and \(x_2\) coffees for \(\$26\) total revenue, and sold \(10\) drinks in all. Write the two equations and the matrix form. Square?
W4. Anticipating outcomes. Without fully solving, say what you expect (and why) for:

\(2\) equations, \(2\) unknowns, with clearly parallel incompatible lines.
\(1\) equation, \(3\) unknowns: \(x_1+x_2+x_3=5\).
\(3\) equations, \(2\) unknowns that happen to be consistent (e.g. the third is the sum of the first two).

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Your turn
Y1. Write as \(Ax=b\): \[
\begin{aligned}
3x_1 - x_2 &= 0 \\
x_1 + 4x_2 &= 7.
\end{aligned}
\] Classify as square / over / under.
Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). For \(b=(1,1,2)\), explain in one sentence why \(Ax=b\) has a solution, and give one solution \(x\).
Y3. True or false, with a one-line reason: every square system \(Ax=b\) has exactly one solution.
Y4. A sensor gives \(4\) linear measurements for \(2\) unknown parameters. Is the system typically overdetermined? Does that guarantee inconsistency?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\1&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}0\\7\end{bmatrix}.
\] Square (\(m=n=2\)).
Y2. \(b=1\cdot a_1+1\cdot a_2\), so \(b\) is in the column span; one solution is \(x=(1,1)\).
Y3. False. Square systems can be inconsistent (parallel lines) or have infinitely many solutions (same line twice).
Y4. Typically overdetermined (\(m=4>n=2\)). No — consistency depends on whether \(b\) lands in a \(2\)-dimensional column space; it might or might not.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Warm-up
For the system \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + 2x_2 &= 5 \\

\end{aligned}
\] write the augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\). What does each row mean as an equation?

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Fill in
The augmented matrix of \(Ax=b\) is the matrix \([A\mid b]\) with \(A\) on the left and \(b\) as an extra \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Elementary row operations (EROs) that do not change the solution set:

\(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) two rows.
Multiply a row by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) scalar.
Add a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of one row to another row.

Why they preserve solutions: each ERO is reversible (undo with another ERO), so the new system is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to the old one — same solution set.
Gaussian elimination aims for (row) echelon form: zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) each pivot, pivots marching right as you go down. Then back substitution solves from the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation upward.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Worked in class
W1. One ERO. Starting from \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 3 & | & 8
\end{bmatrix},
\] replace Row 2 by (Row 2) \(-\) \(2\cdot\)(Row 1). Write the new matrix and the matching equation for the new Row 2.
W2. Finish and back-substitute. Continue W1 to echelon form, then solve for \(x_2\) and \(x_1\).
W3. A \(3\times 3\) warm-up. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & | & 5
\end{bmatrix}
\] to echelon form (you choose the EROs). Do not fully RREF unless time; stop when back substitution is clear. Solve.
W4. Why not “just swap randomly”? Explain in one sentence why multiplying a row by \(0\) is not an allowed ERO for solving systems.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Your turn
Y1. Augmented matrix for \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - x_2 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 &= 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Y2. Perform one elimination step: clear the \((2,1)\) entry of \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\] by a row replacement. Write the new matrix.
Y3. From the echelon form \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix},
\] solve by back substitution.
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: if you swap two rows of \([A\mid b]\), the solution set of \(Ax=b\) can change.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y2. Row2 \(\leftarrow\) Row2 \(-\) \(3\cdot\)Row1 gives \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y3. From Row 2: \(5x_2=9\) so \(x_2=9/5\). From Row 1: \(x_1-x_2=1\) so \(x_1=1+9/5=14/5\). Solution \(x=(14/5,\,9/5)\).
Y4. False. Swapping rows is an elementary row operation; it reorders equations but keeps the same solution set.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Fill in
Reduced row echelon form (RREF) is echelon form with these extras:

Each pivot is \(\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\).
Each pivot is the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) nonzero in its column (zeros above and below).

A pivot variable (basic variable) corresponds to a pivot column. A free variable has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) pivot in its column; assign a parameter (e.g. \(x_3=t\)).
Reading the RREF of \([A\mid b]\):







Pattern
Conclusion




A row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\)
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)


Every column of \(A\) has a pivot, and consistent
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution


Consistent, and at least one free variable
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) solutions



Software. Use a solver or RREF command (Octave rref, Python SymPy rref, or a course helper). Always verify a candidate \(x\) by computing the residual \(Ax-b\) (should be near \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)).

text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify from RREF (no original system needed).

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}

0 & 0 & | & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}

0 & 0 & 1 & | & 4
\end{bmatrix}
\]

W2. Parametric form. From \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix},
\] identify free variable(s) and write \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in terms of parameter(s).
W3. Software + residual. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\11\end{bmatrix},
\] solve \(Ax=b\) with Octave or Python. Compute \(Ax-b\) and confirm it is (numerically) zero.
Octave sketch: A\[b] or rref([A b]) then read \(x\).
Python sketch: np.linalg.solve(A,b) for square invertible \(A\), or SymPy Matrix.hstack(A,b).rref().
W4. Inconsistent check. Invent a \(2\times 2\) augmented RREF that is inconsistent. What would \(Ax-b\) look like if software “forced” a least-squares answer? (One sentence — foreshadow Week 15.)

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Your turn
Y1. From RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 & | & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 3 & | & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\] list pivot variables, free variables, and the general solution.
Y2. True or false: if RREF has a row of all zeros including the augmented entry, the system is inconsistent.
Y3. You solve \(Ax=b\) in software and get \(x=(1,-1)\). You compute \(Ax-b=(0.0,\,10^{-15})\). Was the solve successful? Why check the residual?
Y4. A \(3\times 5\) matrix \(A\) (after RREF of \([A\mid b]\), consistent) has \(3\) pivots. How many free variables? Unique solution or infinitely many?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Pivot variables \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). Then \(x_1-2t=5\) and \(x_2+3t=-1\), so \[
x=(5+2t,\,-1-3t,\,t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Y2. False. A zero row including the right-hand side is consistent (redundant equation). Inconsistency needs \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\).
Y3. Yes — residual is numerically zero (roundoff). Checking \(Ax-b\) catches wrong \(x\), singular/ill-conditioned cases, and copy-paste mistakes.
Y4. \(n=5\) unknowns and \(3\) pivots \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\) free variables \(\Rightarrow\) infinitely many solutions (when consistent).

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems

Learning objectives
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Warm-up
From Lecture 19, the matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] sends (urban, rural) population fractions today to tomorrow. If today’s state is \(x_0=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(x_1=Ax_0\). In one sentence: what do the two entries of \(x_1\) mean?

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Fill in
A linear dynamical system (discrete time) has the form \[
x_{t+1}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}},
\] where \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\) is the time index.

The state \(x_t\) is an \(n\)-vector that completely describes the system at time \(t\).
The matrix \(A\) is the dynamics / transition matrix. Its size is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (same \(n\) as the state).

Interpretation of columns. The \(j\)th column of \(A\) is the next state if the current state is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (one unit in compartment \(j\), nothing elsewhere).
A few steps by hand. \[
x_1=Ax_0,\qquad x_2=Ax_1=A(Ax_0),\qquad x_3=Ax_2=\cdots.
\] (We will package “\(t\) steps at once” as \(A^t\) later; today focus on one step at a time.)
Building \(A\) from a flow story. For each compartment \(j\), ask: if everything starts in \(j\), where does it go next? Those destinations become column \(j\).

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Worked in class
W1. State and matrix. A campus tracks (on-campus residents, off-campus) each week as a \(2\)-vector \(x_t\). Someone proposes \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.15\\ 0.3&0.85\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) What does entry \(A_{12}\) mean in words? (b) What does the first column of \(A\) represent? (c) If \(x_0=(800,200)\), compute \(x_1\) and interpret both entries (people, not fractions).
W2. Build \(A\) from flows. Two towns, Arcata and Eureka, exchange residents each year:

Of those in Arcata, \(80\%\) stay and \(20\%\) move to Eureka.
Of those in Eureka, \(90\%\) stay and \(10\%\) move to Arcata.

Order the state as \(x_t=(\text{Arcata},\text{Eureka})\). Write the \(2\times 2\) transition matrix \(A\).
W3. Next few states. With \(A\) from W2 and \(x_0=(5000,7000)\), compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by hand. Does the Arcata population rise or fall over these two years?
W4. Epidemic sketch (Boyd-style). Let \(x_t=(S_t,I_t)\) be (susceptible, infected) counts among a fixed population of size \(N=S_t+I_t\). A simple model uses \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.95&0.10\\ 0.05&0.90\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Check that each column sums to \(1\). Why is that natural here? (b) If \(x_0=(190,10)\), compute \(x_1\). Did infections go up or down?

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Your turn
Y1. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), then knowing \(x_t\) and \(A\) determines \(x_{t+1}\) uniquely.
Y2. Three age groups (youth, adult, senior) with transition \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 & 0 & 0 \\
0.4 & 0.7 & 0 \\
0 & 0.3 & 0.8
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Interpret \(A_{21}\) and \(A_{33}\) in one phrase each. If \(x_0=(100,200,50)\), compute \(x_1\).
Y3. Build \(A\). Two warehouse inventory levels \(x_t=(\text{A},\text{B})\). Each day:

Warehouse A keeps \(70\%\) of its stock and ships \(30\%\) to B.
Warehouse B keeps \(60\%\) and ships \(40\%\) to A.

Write \(A\). Then with \(x_0=(100,50)\), find \(x_1\).
Y4. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(2,8)\), compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Which component is growing? Which is shrinking?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. True. The rule \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) is a function of the current state: one matrix–vector product gives the unique next state.
Y2. \(A_{21}=0.4\): fraction (or count factor) of youth that become adults in one step. \(A_{33}=0.8\): fraction of seniors that remain seniors. \[
x_1=Ax_0=\begin{bmatrix}60\\180\\100\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y3. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.4\\ 0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x_1=\begin{bmatrix}90\\60\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Column 1: keep \(70\%\) in A, ship \(30\%\) to B. Column 2: ship \(40\%\) of B to A, keep \(60\%\) in B.)
Y4. \(x_1=(2.2,4)\), \(x_2=(2.42,2)\). First component grows (factor \(1.1\) each step); second shrinks (factor \(0.5\)).

Learning objectives

Conduct a simple what-if simulation.

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Warm-up
With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\ 0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by hand. Guess (no calculator marathon): after many steps, will \(x_t\) blow up, shrink to zero, or settle somewhere nonzero?

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Fill in
Simulation recipe (any language):

Choose \(A\) and initial state \(x_0\).
For \(t=0,1,\ldots,T-1\): set \(x_{t+1}=\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Store or plot the components of \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_T\) versus time.

Long-run patterns (names only — recognize from plots / tables):







Pattern
What you see




Stabilization
\(x_t\) approaches a fixed vector (or settles in magnitude)


Growth
components grow without bound (often roughly geometric)


Decay
components shrink toward \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Oscillation
components bounce / cycle in sign or value



What-if. Change one thing — a parameter inside \(A\), or the initial state \(x_0\) — and re-simulate. Compare the two trajectories.
Limitations of \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\). The model is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (no \(x^2\) terms, no products of states); \(A\) is assumed constant; time is discrete; there is no noise, capacity limit, or policy change unless you build it into \(A\). Real systems may only match the model for a while.

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Worked in class
W1. Many steps on the board / laptop. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute (or run) \(x_1\) through \(x_5\). Sketch each component versus \(t\). Does the trajectory look like growth, decay, oscillation, or stabilization?
W2. Recognize the pattern. Without naming any fancy theory, match each matrix to the most plausible long-run story for a generic nonzero \(x_0\):

\(A=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\)
\(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)
\(A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix}\)

W3. What-if. Same \(A\) as W1, but start from \(x_0=(0,1)\) instead of \((1,0)\). Compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Do the two initial conditions seem headed toward the same long-run mix, or different ones?
W4. Limitations. A linear infection model \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with fixed \(A\) predicts infections forever according to the same rule. Name two real-world reasons this could fail after a few weeks (policy, behavior, medicine, saturation, …).

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Your turn
Y1. Simulation plan. Write 3–4 lines of pseudocode (or Octave/Python if you prefer) that, given \(A\) and \(x_0\), prints \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{10}\).
Y2. Pattern ID. You simulate \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) and obtain the first component sequence \[
3,\; -3,\; 3,\; -3,\; 3,\;\ldots
\] Which pattern name fits best? Give one \(2\times 2\) matrix that could produce oscillation like this from \(x_0=(3,0)\) (many answers OK; one simple choice is enough).
Y3. What-if. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(0.5,\,0.5)\) and \(x_0=(8,2)\).

Compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by hand.
If instead \(x_0=(80,20)\), how do \(x_1,x_2\) compare? What limitation / feature of linearity does this illustrate?

Y4. Conjecture (no proof needed). For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix},
\] compare long-run behavior starting from \(x_0=(1,0)\) versus \(x_0=(0,1)\). Write one sentence you want explained later in the course.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Example pseudocode:
x ← x0
print x
for t = 1 to 10:
    x ← A x
    print x
(Octave: x = A*x in a for loop; Python: x = A @ x.)
Y2. Oscillation. One simple choice: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) (or \(A=-I\), or a \(180^\circ\) rotation), which sends \((3,0)\mapsto(-3,0)\mapsto(3,0)\mapsto\cdots\).
Y3. (a) \(x_1=(4,1)\), \(x_2=(2,0.5)\). (b) \(x_1=(40,10)\), \(x_2=(20,5)\) — exactly \(10\times\) the previous trajectory. Linearity scales the whole path with the initial state; the model has no “saturation” that would break that scaling.
Y4. Sample conjecture: from \((1,0)\) the state grows without bound along the first axis; from \((0,1)\) it decays to zero — so long-run fate seems to depend on the direction of \(x_0\), not just its size. (Week 13 will explain this with eigenvectors.)

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What are the dimensions of \(A\) and of \(B\)? Is \(AB\) defined? If so, what size is it?
Compute \(Bx\) (a \(2\)-vector). You will need this later as “\(B\) first, then \(A\).”

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Fill in
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\), the product \(AB\) is the \(m\times p\) matrix whose \(j\)th column is \[
(AB)_j = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] Equivalently, entry \((i,j)\) is the inner product of \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(A\) with \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(B\): \[
(AB)_{ij} = a_i^{\mathsf{T}} b_j.
\]
When is \(AB\) defined? The inner dimensions must match: number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(A\) equals number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(B\).
Associativity (for vectors). For a compatible \(p\)-vector \(x\), \[
(AB)x = A(Bx).
\] Reading right to left: apply \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) first, then \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\). So \(ABx\) is a sequence of transformations.
Not commutative. In general \(AB\neq BA\) (even when both products are defined). Order of maps matters: “rotate then reflect” is not the same as “reflect then rotate.”

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Worked in class
W1. Dimensions. For each pair, decide whether \(AB\) is defined and give the size of \(AB\) if it is.

\(A\) is \(3\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 3\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 2\).

W2. Compute a product. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(AB\) by forming columns \(Ab_1\) and \(Ab_2\) (or by row–column inner products).
W3. Sequence of maps. Using the same \(A\), \(B\), and \(x=(1,-1)\) from the warm-up, compute \(Bx\), then \(A(Bx)\). Compare with \((AB)x\) using your \(AB\) from W2. Same answer?
W4. Non-commutativity. With the same \(A\) and \(B\), compute \(BA\). Is \(BA=AB\)?

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
D=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Is \(CD\) defined? Size? Compute \(CD\).
Y2. Is \(DC\) defined? If so, give its size (you need not compute every entry unless time allows). What does this say about “\(CD\) vs \(DC\)”?
Y3. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW) and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) (horizontal stretch). Compute \(RSx\) and \(SRx\) for \(x=(1,0)\). Same point? Interpret in one sentence.
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(AB\) and \(BA\) are both defined, then \(A\) and \(B\) must be square of the same size.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), \(D\) is \(3\times 2\), so \(CD\) is defined and \(2\times 2\): \[
CD=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Columns: \(Cd_1=(-2,1)\), \(Cd_2=(2,2)\).)
Y2. Yes — \(D\) is \(3\times 2\) and \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), so \(DC\) is \(3\times 3\). Even when both products exist they need not have the same size, so they cannot be equal as matrices. Order matters.
Y3. \(Sx=(2,0)\), then \(RSx=(0,2)\). Meanwhile \(Rx=(0,1)\), then \(SRx=(0,1)\). Different: stretch-then-rotate \(\neq\) rotate-then-stretch for this \(x\).
Y4. False. Example: \(A\) is \(2\times 3\) and \(B\) is \(3\times 2\) — both \(AB\) (\(2\times 2\)) and \(BA\) (\(3\times 3\)) are defined, but neither factor is square. (They become the same size only when \(m=n\).)
